title: Review: Chemistry — Pure and impure substances
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for KS3 Science (chemistry) (status of the source: authored-reviewed-reverified-2026-10-08). Terms and clues: C3.1#xt2 term and clue written for the game; C3#c03 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C3.3#xt1 term and clue written for the game; C3#c06 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. Questions: C3#q02, C3#q07, C3#x02 (written for the game), C3#q15, C3#q19, C3#q04, C3#q05, C3#q11, C3#q18, C3#q21, C3#x01 (written for the game), C3#q06. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Purity
items.clue: A measure of how much of a sample is the one wanted substance

items.label: Mixture
items.clue: Two or more substances that are together but not chemically joined.

items.label: Diffusion
items.clue: Particles spreading out and mixing because of their own random movement.

items.label: Solvent
items.clue: The liquid that the solute dissolves in, for example the water in salty water.

questions.stem: A label says 'Pure spring water: natural, with nothing added'. Spring water has minerals dissolved in it. What is it to a scientist?

options.text: A mixture of water and minerals
A pure substance, as it is natural
A pure substance, as it looks so clear
A compound of water and minerals

questions.explanation: Yes. It contains water and dissolved minerals, which are not joined, so it is a mixture. To a scientist it is not pure.

questions.stem: Salt is stirred into water until no more will dissolve. More salt is then added, at the same temperature. What happens to the extra salt, and why?

options.text: It stays solid, as salt is insoluble
It stays solid in the saturated solution
It dissolves if you stir for longer
It melts away into the salty water

questions.explanation: Yes. The solution is saturated: it holds as much salt as can dissolve at that temperature, so the extra salt stays as solid at the bottom.

questions.stem: Diffusion is much faster in gases than in liquids. Which explains this, using the particle model?

options.text: Gas particles move quickly through large gaps
Gas particles are smaller than liquid ones
Gas particles are carried along by air currents
Gas particles try to spread themselves out evenly

questions.explanation: Gas particles move quickly and are far apart, so they travel further between collisions and mix faster.

questions.stem: You want to get back both the water and the salt from salty water. Which method should you use?

options.text: Separate it by distillation
Separate it by evaporation
Separate it by filtration
Separate it by chromatography

questions.explanation: Yes. Distillation boils off the water and cools the vapour in a condenser to collect it as pure water, while the salt stays behind in the flask.

questions.stem: How does a pure solid melt?

options.text: Over a range of temperatures
At 0 °C, just as ice does
Only at a very hot temperature
At exactly one temperature

questions.explanation: Yes. A pure solid melts at one sharp, fixed temperature, its melting point. The temperature stays the same until it has all melted.

questions.stem: Rock salt is dug from the ground. Salt is extracted from it by dissolving, filtering and evaporating. Which is purer, and why?

options.text: The rock salt, as it is natural and untouched
The rock salt, as extracting is a chemical change
Both are equally pure, as both are just salt
The extracted salt, as the rock and soil are removed

questions.explanation: Yes. Dissolving and filtering leave the insoluble rock and soil behind, so the extracted salt contains far fewer other substances. It is the same salt, just separated from the rest.

questions.stem: Sugar is added to water and dissolves. This makes a sugar solution. Which is the solute?

options.text: The water it dissolves in
The sugar solution as a whole
The sugar that dissolves
Nothing, as the sugar has gone

questions.explanation: Yes. The solute is the substance that dissolves, here the sugar. The water is the solvent, and the sugar solution is the mixture made.

questions.stem: In the particle model, what causes diffusion?

options.text: Particles that want to spread out
A push from wind or stirring
Particles reacting with each other
Particles moving about at random

questions.explanation: Yes. Particles in liquids and gases move about all the time in all directions. This random movement makes them spread out and mix, with nothing pushing them.

questions.stem: A mixture contains sand, salt and water. Which plan gives dry salt with no sand in it?

options.text: Filter, then evaporate the liquid that comes through
Evaporate first, then filter the dry solid that is left
Filter, then scrape the salt off the filter paper
Distil, then collect the salt that drips out

questions.explanation: Yes. Filtering traps the insoluble sand while the dissolved salt passes through with the water. Evaporating that filtrate then leaves the salt as dry crystals.

questions.stem: Two inks are tested by paper chromatography. Ink S gives one spot. Ink T gives three spots. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: S is a mixture, and T may be pure
Both are pure, since each is one ink
T's dyes were made by the test
S may be pure; T is a mixture

questions.explanation: Yes. A pure substance gives only one spot, so S may be pure (more tests would check). T separates into three spots, so it contains at least three dyes: it is a mixture.

questions.stem: To a scientist, which of these is a pure substance?

options.text: Clean mountain air
Fresh orange juice
Carbon dioxide gas
Filtered sea water

questions.explanation: A pure substance is a single element or compound; air, juice and sea water are all mixtures.

questions.stem: Sugar is stirred into hot tea until it can no longer be seen. What has happened to the sugar?

options.text: It has melted and become liquid sugar
It has gone and is no longer in the tea
It reacted with water to make a new compound
Its particles have spread out in the water

questions.explanation: Yes. The sugar has dissolved: its particles have spread out among the water particles. The sugar is still there, which is why the tea tastes sweet.
